708.title: A roll of honor
708.hook: Var 11 lists the Sikhs of the Gurus by name and town, ordinary people remembered (Bhai Gurdas, Var 11)
708.howItsDone: Sikhs read Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var as a record of the early sangat, and it's read and sung alongside the Gurus' bani in some gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angad: Nanak bowed to his own disciple, light merging into light. Today, the people who sat around the Gurus.

On the wall of an old school hallway, or a fire station, or a village hall, there's often a board with names painted on it in gold. Hardly anyone stops to read it. But somebody once decided those names should outlast the people. Bhai Gurdas made a board like that, out of verse. One of his vars stops telling the stories of the Gurus and starts telling the names of the people who sat with them. Today: sangat.
screen: `NAMES PAINTED IN GOLD.` → `HARDLY ANYONE STOPS TO READ THEM.` → `A BOARD MADE OUT OF VERSE.`

segments.voice: It's his eleventh var. Bhai Gurdas begins with the sangat, the gathering of the Guru's Sikhs, and what a Sikh of the Guru is like. Then he does something a reader might not expect. He starts listing names. Sikh after Sikh, Guru by Guru, he names the people who came to Guru Nanak, then to the Gurus after him. Often a name comes with something attached: the town they came from, their family, their trade, a nickname their neighbors would have known. Read it and you meet a crowd of ordinary people. Not kings, not famous holy men. People with work to do and towns to go home to. Why would a poet spend so many stanzas on a list? Here's one way to hear it. A story about a great teacher can blur the followers into a background crowd that nods. Bhai Gurdas refuses the blur. For him, the sangat isn't scenery around the Guru. It's made of particular people, each worth a line, each named the way their own town would have named them. And a list like this is a kind of witness. These people were there. They heard the Guru's word, carried it home, and lived it in their own streets. One more thing. In the Guru's house, a name on the roll doesn't depend on rank. In Bhai Gurdas's list, being remembered comes from being a Sikh of the Guru. That's the whole qualification.

709.title: What a Gursikh does
709.hook: Bhai Gurdas pictures the Sikh who rises early, bathes, remembers, joins the sangat and works honestly
709.howItsDone: Sikh custom keeps the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, for bathing and reciting or listening to the morning banis before the day's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat: Bhai Gurdas's roll of ordinary Sikhs, each one named. Today, the shape of their day.

What would a stranger learn about you from watching one ordinary day? Not your opinions. Just the day: what time the light went on, what you did first, where you went, how you earned your bread. Bhai Gurdas gives us the day of a Sikh who belongs to the Guru, and he doesn't describe it with a list of beliefs. He describes it with a clock. Today's word: Gursikh.
screen: `ONE ORDINARY DAY, WATCHED.` → `NOT OPINIONS, JUST THE DAY.` → `A DAY TOLD BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Gursikh puts two words together: Gur, the Guru, and Sikh. A Sikh of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas returns to this person in his vars, and the picture he paints is practical, almost a timetable. The Gursikh rises while the night is still on, in the early hours. Bathes. Then remembers: sits with the Guru's word, with the Name, before the day's noise starts. Then goes to the sangat, to sit with others and hear and sing the Guru's hymns. Then goes to work, earns a living honestly, and shares what comes in. No mountaintop, no cave: a house, a gathering, a workplace. The picture has deep roots in the Guru's own word. On Ang three hundred five of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru: rising early, bathing, meditating on the Name, and carrying the Guru's word through the rest of the day. Bhai Gurdas fills in the day around that morning. Three things stand out. First, the order. Remembering comes before the work, so the work happens inside the remembering, not instead of it. Second, the company. The Gursikh's day isn't solitary: the sangat is part of the schedule, not an extra. Third, the money. Honest work is in the picture on purpose. Holiness doesn't leave the marketplace; it walks into it with clean hands. A Gursikh, in this telling, isn't known by a title. You'd know one by watching the day.

710.title: One, two, five
710.hook: Bhai Gurdas says one Sikh is a Sikh, two are a sangat, and where five gather the Lord is present (Bhai Gurdas, Var 13)
710.howItsDone: Sikhs gather in sangats of every size, from a family reading together at home to a full gurdwara, and Bhai Gurdas's line is quoted for the worth of even a small gathering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gursikh, and a day told by the clock: remembering first, then the sangat, then honest work. Today, a line that counts.

One chair by a window, someone reading alone. A second chair pulled up, and now there's a conversation. Three more, and suddenly it's a gathering, and the room feels different. Nothing about the furniture changed. Bhai Gurdas noticed what changes when people add up, and he put it in a line short enough to say in a single breath, a line that simply counts, the way a child counts on her fingers. Today: one, two, five.
screen: `ONE CHAIR BY A WINDOW.` → `A SECOND CHAIR: A CONVERSATION.` → `FIVE CHAIRS: A GATHERING.`

segments.voice: It's in his thirteenth var. Bhai Gurdas says: one is a Sikh. Two are a sadh sangat, a holy company. And where five are, there is God. Take the steps one at a time. One is a Sikh. A single person, alone, early in the morning, remembering, is already a Sikh. Nobody needs a crowd to be on the path. Two are a sangat. The moment a second person joins, it's no longer just practice. It's company. Two people reading a line of the Guru's word together, or singing it softly in a kitchen, already make the thing Bhai Gurdas praises in his vars. And then, five. Where five gather, he says, God is present. Not that God is absent from the one, or the two. The line climbs, the way a person climbs stairs, and at the top is the plainest promise of the three. Some readers hear in it an old Punjabi way of speaking about a village council of five, where God was said to sit among the five. Some also hear it ahead of a moment later in the Sikh story, when five Sikhs stand together at the heart of the Khalsa. Bhai Gurdas doesn't spell out either one. His line simply counts. What's striking is how small his numbers are. He doesn't say a thousand, or a full gurdwara, or a festival crowd. He says five: a gathering that fits around one table. In Bhai Gurdas's arithmetic, the holy company was never about size. It starts with one, becomes real with two, and five is enough.

711.title: A hedge round the orchard
711.hook: defending Guru Hargobind's new ways, Bhai Gurdas says an orchard needs a thorny hedge (Bhai Gurdas, Var 26)
711.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind for holding miri and piri together, worldly and spiritual authority, and Bhai Gurdas's twenty-sixth var is read as an early defense of that change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one, two, five: one is a Sikh, two a holy company, and where five gather, there is God. Today, a hedge of thorns.

Nobody plants a hedge of thorns for its own sake. Thorn bushes aren't pretty, and they snag your sleeve. But walk around an old orchard, with fruit hanging low and goats wandering nearby, and the thorns suddenly make sense. They were never there for themselves. They were there for the fruit. Bhai Gurdas reached for exactly that picture when people were troubled by a Guru who didn't look like the Gurus before him. Today: kikar.
screen: `NOBODY PLANTS THORNS FOR FUN.` → `AN ORCHARD, AND GOATS NEARBY.` → `A GURU WHO LOOKED DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: The Guru was Guru Hargobind. Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who took up the sword alongside the Guru's word, and kept horses and armed Sikhs around him. And some people didn't like it. In his twenty-sixth var, Bhai Gurdas sets out what they were saying, and he doesn't soften it. The earlier Gurus sat in the dharamsal, they said, and this one doesn't stay in one place. He keeps dogs. He goes hunting. The Gurus before him gave us hymns; this one doesn't sit and compose them. Bhai Gurdas lets the complaints stand in full. Then he answers. The truth, he says, can't be hidden, and the Sikhs still gather round the Guru like bees round a lotus. And then the picture that names today. To protect an orchard, you plant a hedge of thorny kikar around it. The hedge isn't the orchard, and it isn't the fruit. Nobody walks into an orchard to admire the thorns. But without them, the fruit doesn't survive the season. Hear what Bhai Gurdas is claiming. The swords and horses aren't a change of heart. The orchard is the same one Nanak planted: the Name, the sangat, the Guru's word. The hedge is what keeps it alive in hard times. It holds together two things people tend to pull apart: gentleness and protection, a path of humility and the readiness to defend it. Sikhs speak of this as miri and piri, the worldly and the spiritual held by the same Guru. Bhai Gurdas says it with a gardener's eye.
screen: `A GURU WITH SWORD AND HORSES.` · `THE COMPLAINTS, IN FULL.` · `A HEDGE OF THORNY KIKAR.` · `THE HEDGE IS NOT THE ORCHARD.` · then, large: `A HEDGE FOR THE ORCHARD.`

segments.voice: Name one good thing growing in your life that's easy to trample: a morning routine, a friendship that's still new, a child's bedtime story, an hour that's meant to be yours. Then ask what small hedge would keep it safe, not a wall, just a phone left in another room, a no said kindly, a time written down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over the thing you're guarding.
Kikar, the thorny tree Bhai Gurdas pictures hedging an orchard: the orchard needs it to keep the fruit alive, answering those troubled by Guru Hargobind's new ways.
Your line: a hedge for the orchard. The thorns were never the point; the fruit was. See you tomorrow.

712.title: The kabitts
712.hook: Bhai Gurdas also wrote short Braj verses of great beauty
712.howItsDone: Bhai Gurdas's Kabitt Savaiye are studied and recited by Sikhs alongside his vars, and some are sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kikar: the thorny hedge that guards the orchard Nanak planted. Today, Bhai Gurdas's other voice.

Some writers have two voices. The same person who writes a long novel also scribbles tiny poems in the margins, and sometimes it's the tiny ones people carry around. For days now we've been walking through Bhai Gurdas's vars: long ballads, stanza after stanza, telling the story of the Gurus and the sangat. But that wasn't all he wrote. He had a second voice, in a second language, and it was small. Today: the kabitts.
screen: `TWO VOICES, ONE WRITER.` → `THE LONG BALLADS: THE VARS.` → `A SECOND VOICE, SMALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the language. The vars are in Punjabi. The kabitts are in Braj, a language of poetry, written down in the Gurmukhi script Sikhs use for the Guru's word. Bhai Gurdas could move between them. Then the shape. A kabitt is a short, tightly measured stanza. Where a var tells a story across many verses, a kabitt has to say what it says inside one. It can't wander. It packs. One way Bhai Gurdas packs is by stacking pictures. As this, so that. As a thing in nature behaves, so a Sikh of the Guru behaves. Comparison after comparison, pressed close together, until the last line lands with all their weight behind it. A kabitt is less like a road and more like a jewel: you turn it over in your hand and the light catches a different face each time. Why does that matter? Because some truths need a story, and some need a stone you can carry. One way to hear it: the vars suit a long evening in the sangat, when there's time for the whole tale. The kabitts suit a pocket: short enough to learn, dense enough to keep giving. And there's a quiet lesson in the fact that he wrote both. The same devotion can be told long and told short: a whole life of praise, and a single bright line you can read aloud before the kettle boils.

713.title: Bhai Nand Lal
713.hook: a Persian poet and scholar who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court
713.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems, and Sikh custom allows them, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, in kirtan alongside the Guru's bani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kabitts: Bhai Gurdas's short verses in Braj, small and bright. Today, a second teller.

Bhai Gurdas has been our guide since this year began, writing in Punjabi and in Braj, close to the Gurus who came before. Now the path hands us to a second teller, from a later court and a different language. He's a learned man who writes in Persian, the language Rumi and Hafiz wrote in, and he spends his gift on Guru Gobind Singh. Sikhs know him by a title of respect, and by a pen name. Today: Goya.
screen: `A SECOND TELLER.` → `A LATER COURT, A NEW LANGUAGE.` → `PERSIAN, FOR THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bhai Nand Lal was a poet and a scholar who served at the court of Guru Gobind Singh. Bhai is the same title of respect Bhai Gurdas carries: brother. He wrote under a pen name, Goya, in the Persian manner, and what he wrote, he wrote in Persian. Here's the thing to notice. A court in his world was a place of learning and display, and Persian poetry was a high art, with its own rules, its own pictures, its own long tradition of writing about love for the Divine as a lover writes about the beloved. Nand Lal didn't leave that behind when he came to the Guru. He didn't decide that a Sikh had to stop being a poet, or stop writing in the language he'd mastered. He turned the whole art toward the Guru. The lover, the beloved, the beloved's face: in his poems, those old Persian pictures point to the One, and to the Guru who shows the way. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gathered poets around him, and Nand Lal is one of the names Sikhs remember. His learning wasn't treated as a distraction from devotion. It became a way of devotion. Over the next few days you'll meet some of his writing: a book about life, his love poems, and writings on conduct that carry his name. Today, just meet the man: a scholar at court, a poet with a pen name, who brought the best thing he had, his Persian, and laid it at the Guru's feet. Sikh custom lets his poems, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, be sung in kirtan.

714.title: The book of life
714.hook: Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama speaks of the longing to see the Beloved in everything
714.howItsDone: Sikhs read Bhai Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama in Persian and in translation, and its verses are recited and sung as poems of longing for the Divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goya, the pen name of Bhai Nand Lal, who turned his Persian art toward the Guru. Today, one of his books.

Someone who's just fallen in love sees the beloved's name on a shop sign. Hears their laugh in a stranger's voice across a train platform. Smells their coat in a crowded elevator. The world hasn't changed. The one looking at it has. Bhai Nand Lal took that ordinary, slightly ridiculous experience, made it into a whole way of seeing, and pointed it at God. He gave the book a plain title. Today: Zindagi Nama.
screen: `A NAME ON A SHOP SIGN.` → `THE WORLD HASN'T CHANGED.` → `THE ONE LOOKING HAS.`

segments.voice: Zindagi means life. Nama, a book or a letter. The book of life. It's a poem, written in Persian, in the language of love poetry. Here is its center. Nand Lal writes of a longing to see the Beloved, meaning God, and of the strange thing that happens when that longing takes hold: the Beloved begins to show up everywhere, wherever the eye falls. For the one who longs, there's nowhere the Beloved isn't. Turn that over a few ways. First, the longing isn't a problem to be cured. In the Zindagi Nama, wanting to see is itself part of the path. The ache is a kind of attention. Second, the seeing is the reward. Not a vision in a far-off place, not a reward after death. A changed way of looking, here, at ordinary things. Third, it fits the Guru's word Nand Lal knew. Sikhs hear the Guru Granth Sahib speak of the One pervading everything, in every heart, in water and land. Nand Lal says it in the language of a lover who can't stop seeing the beloved's face. And fourth, it's for a life, not a moment. The title says so: a book of life, a way to walk through all of it with your eyes open. Nand Lal doesn't promise the longing ever goes quiet. He seems to treat it as a good companion for the whole road.

When your eyes want to move on, stay one breath longer, and if you pray, you can say Waheguru to what you see.
